title: Emotions & Relationships Shorts · Episode 1
chapters: Laughter: it's not really about jokes
Nostalgia: why we long for the good old days

units.t: Emotions & Relationships Shorts. Episode one.
In this episode: Laughter: it's not really about jokes, Nostalgia: why we long for the good old days and Why we cry.
Part one. Laughter: it's not really about jokes.
We think we laugh because something is funny.
One scientist spent years eavesdropping on laughing strangers and found that most laughter has nothing to do with humour at all.
Laughter isn't about jokes.
In the 1990s neuroscientist Robert Provine, of the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, took a simple approach.
Rather than showing people comedy in a lab, he and his students hung around shopping centres, campuses and city streets, noting what people had just said when someone laughed.
Across more than a thousand episodes, only around 10 to 20 per cent of laughs followed anything like a joke.
Most came after lines such as 'I'll see you guys later' or 'Are you sure?'
Speakers also laughed more than their listeners.
Laughter, Provine concluded, is less a reaction to comedy than a social signal: a way of saying we are friendly, relaxed and on the same side.
Laughter is for company.
If laughter were just about funny things, you would laugh as much alone as with friends.
You don't.

In diary studies, Provine found people laughed about 30 times more often in social situations than alone, and much of what they laughed at alone came from television or radio, which supply a kind of company.
Laughter is also contagious.

Hearing others laugh makes us more likely to laugh, which is why television producers began adding canned laughter in the 1950s, using a machine nicknamed the 'laff box', invented by sound engineer Charley Douglass.
Most people say they dislike laugh tracks, yet studies have found they can make people laugh more at the same jokes.
Older than words.
Laughter is far older than language.
Chimpanzees, bonobos, gorillas and orangutans make breathy panting sounds when they play-wrestle or are tickled.
Researchers who compared these sounds found a family tree of laughter that matches the apes' evolutionary relationships.
Ape laughter pants in and out with each breath, while human laughter chops a single outward breath into rhythmic 'ha-ha-ha' bursts.
The roots may go deeper.
In the late 1990s neuroscientist Jaak Panksepp found that rats make high-pitched chirps, too high for human ears, when tickled, and tickled rats chase the researcher's hand for more.
In mammals, laughter seems to have begun as a signal that rough play is only play.
Real and fake.
Neuroscientist Sophie Scott, of University College London, separates spontaneous laughter, which bursts out of us, from volitional laughter, the polite laugh we produce on purpose.
Brain imaging shows partly different areas respond to each, and people can usually tell them apart.
In a 2014 study by Gregory Bryant and Athena Aktipis, sped-up spontaneous laughs began to sound like animal calls, while deliberate ones still sounded human.
That suggests real laughter relies on an older vocal system than speech does.
Deliberate laughter is not dishonest; it is often a kind, useful signal.
Smiles work similarly.
Guillaume Duchenne, a nineteenth century French neurologist, noted that real joy also tightens the muscle around the eye, creating crow's feet.
But many people can fake this, so it is not a foolproof test.
Good company, not medicine.
Social laughter does something useful.
In 2012 a team led by evolutionary psychologist Robin Dunbar found that people who laughed together at comedy videos could tolerate more pain than those who watched dull films.
They linked this to the brain's own opioid-like chemicals.
Shared laughter helps people feel closer, soothes tension and makes tough situations bearable, as anyone in a hard job with dark humour knows.
But claims that laughter cures disease, or that a set number of laughs replaces exercise, go far beyond the evidence.
Contagion can reach extremes.
In 1962 at a girls' school in Kashasha, Tanganyika, now Tanzania, uncontrollable laughing spread to villages and affected roughly a thousand people over months.
No infection or poison was found; it is described as mass psychogenic illness, a physical response spreading through a group under stress.
The key idea: Studies of everyday conversation found most laughter follows ordinary remarks, because it works as a social signal.
Part two. Nostalgia: why we long for the good old days.
Once considered a dangerous disease, nostalgia turns out to be one of the mind's quiet comforts.
Here is why an old song can make you feel warmer, more connected and more like yourself.
A disease of homesickness.
In 1688 a Swiss medical student, Johannes Hofer, wrote about a strange illness affecting young people far from home, including Swiss soldiers serving abroad.
Sufferers were listless, lost their appetite and pined obsessively for their native mountains.
Hofer coined a word for it by combining the Greek nostos, meaning homecoming, with algos, meaning pain.
Nostalgia literally meant the pain of longing to return home.
For a long time doctors treated it as a serious condition, and some blamed everything from changes in air pressure to the clanging of cowbells.
Over the following centuries the meaning shifted from homesickness for a place to a sentimental longing for the past.
In recent decades, researchers have found that nostalgia is usually far more helpful than harmful.
Bittersweet, mostly sweet.
A song from your first summer job or the smell of your family's beach sunscreen brings warmth tinged with a faint ache.
Research led by Constantine Sedikides and Tim Wildschut at the University of Southampton suggests nostalgia is predominantly positive.
Nostalgic stories often follow a redemption pattern, starting with something hard or ordinary and ending on a positive note, and they tend to feature loved ones.
In experiments, recalling a nostalgic memory, compared with an ordinary one, increased feelings of being loved, raised self-esteem, strengthened a sense of meaning and boosted optimism.
It also builds self-continuity: the sense that today's you is connected to the you of years ago.
In times of change, such as moving, retiring or becoming a parent, that thread is steadying.
A mood repair kit.
Researchers have found that negative feelings, especially loneliness, tend to trigger nostalgia.
When people feel isolated, their minds drift to memories of being close to others, which seems to restore a sense of connection.
Boredom and uncertainty can also prompt nostalgic reflection, perhaps as a way of reaching for meaning.
Some studies even link nostalgia with physical warmth.
In one set of experiments, people felt more nostalgic on colder days, and recalling nostalgic memories seemed to make them feel warmer and more tolerant of cold.
The findings are intriguing rather than definitive, but they fit a pattern.
Nostalgia works like an internal comfort blanket, something the mind reaches for when the present feels a bit chilly.
Why youth looms large.
Ask older adults for important memories or favourite music, and a pattern emerges.
Memories cluster between about age ten and thirty, a phenomenon psychologists call the reminiscence bump.
That period is packed with firsts: first love, first job, first time living away from home.
It is also when people form their adult identity, so those events become part of their life story.
The brain may encode novel, emotional experiences especially well.
This is why the songs of your youth hit differently, and why so many people believe music was better when they were young.
It probably was not better.
It was simply woven into the most formative chapter of your life.
Using nostalgia well.
Marketers, film studios and politicians know nostalgia is persuasive.
Retro packaging, rebooted franchises and 1980s songs in advertisements are no accident.
Nostalgia makes people feel safe and warm, and some research suggests it can make them more willing to spend.
The good old days are also remembered selectively, with hardships trimmed away.
A nostalgic glow is lovely, but it is not a reliable history book.
Some people get stuck comparing a disappointing present with an idealised past, a habit called rosy retrospection.
The trick is to use nostalgia as fuel rather than a refuge: make a playlist from your school years, cook a grandparent's recipe, or message an old friend to share a memory.
Notice, too, tomorrow's nostalgia in today's ordinary moments.
The key idea: Nostalgia was named in 1688 as a medical condition, from Greek words for homecoming and pain.
Part three. Why we cry.
Humans are, as far as scientists can tell, the only animals that shed tears because they feel something.
So why did evolution give us such a strange and visible signal?
Three kinds of tears.
Your eyes are never truly dry.
Small glands keep them coated with basal tears, which wash away dust, feed the cornea and contain proteins that help fight infection.
Every blink spreads a fresh layer.
Reflex tears flood in when something irritates the eye, such as smoke, grit or a chopped onion.
Cutting an onion releases a volatile sulphur compound that irritates nerves in the eye, so the eye flushes it away.
The third type, emotional tears, are the mysterious ones.
Nothing touches the eye.
Sadness, grief, frustration, relief, joy or being deeply moved triggers them.
Humans are, as far as scientists can tell, the only animals that clearly cry for emotional reasons, and thinkers have puzzled over why for centuries.
The plumbing.
The main tear-making organ is the lacrimal gland, tucked under the bony brow above the outer corner of each eye.
Tiny ducts release fluid onto the eye, and blinking sweeps it towards the inner corner.
There, two little openings called puncta, one on each eyelid, act like drains.
They lead to a channel that empties into the nasal cavity.
Normally this system handles the gentle flow of basal tears unnoticed.
When you cry hard, tears are made faster than the drains can cope with, so they spill over the lower lid and down your cheeks.
The extra fluid pouring into your nose explains the sniffing and runny nose that come with a good cry.
A signal to others.
In his 1872 book The Expression of the Emotions in Man and Animals, Charles Darwin studied crying closely, watching his own children among others.
He concluded that weeping was probably incidental, a result of muscles squeezing around the eyes during screaming, rather than useful in itself.
Many later researchers disagree.
Dutch psychologist Ad Vingerhoets, who has studied crying for decades, argues that tears are above all a signal to other people.
Unlike a sob, which anyone nearby can hear, tears are visible mainly up close, to those we are most likely to trust.
They say someone is hurting, overwhelmed or vulnerable, and they tend to draw comfort and help.
Tears may also signal no threat, since blurry eyes and a crumpled face are hard to fight with.
Tears change faces.
In 2009 psychologist Robert Provine and colleagues showed people photos of tearful faces, then the same photos with the tears digitally removed.
With tears, the faces were rated clearly sad.
Without them, many looked far less sad, and some were read as puzzled, concerned or neutral.
Other studies find that people who see tearful faces feel more inclined to help or comfort.
This supports the signal idea.
Adult tears tend to appear in moments of helplessness, and we can find them powerfully moving even in strangers on a screen.
Crying changes across life, too.
Newborns cry loudly from birth, often with few tears at first, because their tear system is still maturing.
Adult triggers shift towards loss, conflict, powerlessness and being moved by kindness or reunion.
Does a good cry help.
Ask people whether crying helps and most say yes.
Yet in laboratories, people watching sad films often feel a little worse straight afterwards.
Some research suggests the lift arrives later, as feelings recover over the following hour or so.
What matters most is what happens around the tears.
People who are comforted or feel understood are more likely to say crying helped.
Those who feel ashamed or judged often feel worse.
A popular claim says tears flush stress chemicals from the body.
Emotional tears differ slightly in make-up, but there is little evidence that so small a volume removes enough of anything to matter.
Crying that rarely stops, or being unable to cry for a long time after a major loss, is worth raising with a GP.
The key idea: Your eyes make basal tears all the time, reflex tears for irritants and emotional tears when feelings run high.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What did Provine's street observations find about what people laughed at?
Answer. Most laughs followed ordinary remarks, not jokes.
Question two. What did the word nostalgia originally describe?
Answer. The pain of longing to return home.
Question three. What triggers emotional tears, unlike reflex tears?
Answer. Feelings such as grief, relief, joy or being moved.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
